doc.title: Mose Allison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Singing like an instrumentalist
summary: Ben Sidran's quote about vocals as accuracy; Allison does not see the trumpet link.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: We’ll do it in half-an-hour. It’s not that much. For Part 3, I’d like to return to some quotes from the past. There’s a 1972 recording called Mose In Your Ear. I thought this was an interesting remark. Ben Sidran, in his liner notes, draws out the comparison between your methods of operation and Thelonious Monk’s methods of operations, which he perceives. There are a couple of things... Amy might have quoted this earlier, and forgive me if I’m repeating it. You said: “It’s all a matter of accuracy,” as far as working off your vocals... “It’s all a matter of accuracy. Whether or not you get the change at the right split second in order to get that hypnotic effect that I’m after. Although I do have personal motivations for certain songs when I’m singing them, they are like cues for myself. I approach most of the vocal parts like an instrumentalist, and that’s the reason it’s important for me to play my own piano background, because it’s all interrelated.” Does that sound like a reasonable...
What are you asking?
I’m asking if that sounds like a reasonable statement of your intentions when you’re playing and accompanying?
That your piano playing and accompanying...
Did you hear what he was reading?
No. I heard some of it.
You’re closer to him. Would you read it. Bottom left.

Ok. It says: “It’s all a matter of accuracy. Whether or not you get the change at the right split second in order to get that hypnotic effect that I’m after. Although I do have personal motivations for certain songs when I’m singing them, they are like cues for myself. I approach most of the vocal parts like an instrumentalist, and that’s the reason it’s important for me to play my own piano background, because it’s all interrelated.” What do you think of that? Does it still apply, do you think?
Do you believe what you said?
Yes, I know. [LAUGHS]
Do you sing like an instrumentalist? When you’re singing a song and phrasing a vocal, is it like it would have been sixty years ago when you were playing that song on trumpet, let’s say?
No. I couldn’t make the transfer from trumpet to piano?
He’s talking about your voice. Is that like an instrument when you’re playing?
I don’t know.
A lot of trumpet players sang. Louis Armstrong. Brass players...
A lot of singers have sounded like horns, kind of.
So I’m wondering if your idea of delivering your voice is similar to the way you’re thinking about projecting an instrument or projecting your breath through the horn?
No. I don’t get anything out of this.
Fair enough.
What about if you were singing and not playing? Would that feel weird, Dad? Maybe playing and singing is interrelated? It’s like part of the same thing?
I don’t know...
What if you weren’t playing and you just sang? Would that feel weird?
Well, who knows?
